body_text: Key takeaways Not all multichannel ecommerce platforms are built for the same purpose. Some are designed for marketplace growth, while others focus on storefront commerce, international expansion, or operational control. The more channels you add, the more important automation becomes. Features like catalog management, inventory synchronization, and workflow automation can help reduce manual work as your business scales. Choosing a platform isn't just about the channels you sell on today. It's also about where you want to grow next and whether your software can support that expansion. The best multichannel software should make selling across channels feel simpler, not add another layer of complexity to your operations. The way consumers shop online has changed dramatically over the past few years. Today's buyers don’t follow a straight path to purchase. They discover products on marketplaces, search engines, social media, and brand websites – often bouncing between several before deciding where to buy. At the same time, converting shoppers still isn’t easy. Global ecommerce websites converted just 1.4% of visitors in Q1 2026, meaning nearly 99% of site traffic didn’t result in a sale . That’s a lot of potential customers slipping through the cracks. Your shoppers are spread across the internet. If you’re only selling in one place, you’re limiting your ability to capture demand wherever it exists. That’s why more brands are embracing a multichannel strategy. By selling across marketplaces like Amazon, Walmart, and Target (alongside their own ecommerce stores), they can reach more customers, diversify their revenue streams, and reduce dependence on any single channel. Of course, expanding to multiple channels creates a new problem: complexity. Product listings need to stay accurate. Inventory needs to stay in sync. Orders need to flow smoothly between systems. And marketplace requirements seem to change every other week. This is where multichannel ecommerce software comes in. The right platform helps centralize listings, inventory, orders, and workflows so your team spends less time managing operational headaches and more time growing the business. What’s the purpose of a multichannel ecommerce software? Managing a single sales channel is challenging enough. Add marketplaces, ecommerce storefronts, and other selling channels into the mix, and things can quickly become difficult to keep track of. Multichannel ecommerce software helps bring those moving pieces together. Rather than logging into multiple systems to manage listings, inventory and orders, brands can centralize key workflows in one place. Today's solutions go well beyond basic listing and inventory management. Many platforms now include catalog management, workflow automation, analytics and marketplace-specific tools designed to help brands operate more efficiently across channels. The biggest benefit goes beyond saving time to creating a more scalable operation. By reducing manual work and improving visibility across channels, the right platform can help sellers grow without adding unnecessary complexity. There are also different types of solutions to consider. Some focus on a specific area of multichannel selling, while others provide a broader set of capabilities that support multiple aspects of ecommerce operations. Key features to look for As you evaluate your options, consider the following features and questions. Download our ecommerce software evaluation checklist to get started. Marketplace connectivity Does the platform support the sales channels that matter most to your business? Not every solution integrates with every marketplace, storefront or operational system. Before committing to a platform, make sure it supports your current channels and any future expansion plans. Catalog & listing management How much manual work is required to create and maintain listings? Every marketplace has unique listing requirements that evolve over time. The best platforms help automate listing creation, updates and optimization so your team can spend less time managing product data. Marketplace change management How quickly can the platform adapt to marketplace changes? Marketplace requirements are constantly evolving. Look for a provider that can help you respond quickly to new policies, listing requirements and channel updates without disrupting day-to-day operations. Inventory synchronization Can the platform keep inventory accurate across channels in real time? Accurate inventory synchronization helps prevent overselling, stockouts and poor customer experiences. Features like inventory buffers can provide an additional layer of protection during periods of high demand. Workflow automation Which repetitive tasks can be automated? The right platform should help reduce manual work by automating routine processes such as catalog updates, listing maintenance, pricing adjustments and other operational workflows. Reporting & analytics Can you easily understand performance across channels? As your channel mix grows, visibility becomes increasingly important. Look for reporting tools that help you identify trends, monitor performance and make informed decisions. Ease of use & support How easy is the platform to learn, and how accessible is the support team? Even the most powerful software can become a burden if it's difficult to use or lacks reliable support. Consider both the user experience and the quality of customer service when evaluating vendors. Top 6 multichannel ecommerce platforms 1. Zentail Best for: Marketplace-first brands looking to streamline operations across Amazon, Walmart, eBay and other major sales channels. Zentail is built specifically for marketplace sellers, combining catalog management, listing automation, inventory synchronization, and workflow automation in a single platform designed to support marketplace growth. The platform helps sellers manage product data, listings and day-to-day operations from one place rather than juggling multiple systems. One of Zentail's biggest differentiators is its SMART Types technology , which helps automate product categorization and listing creation across channels. It also places a strong emphasis on marketplace change management, helping sellers adapt to new marketplace requirements and listing standards while reducing the manual work required to keep products compliant and optimized. Strengths Built specifically for marketplace sellers Automated catalog and listing management Marketplace change management capabilities Workflow automation and bulk editing tools Inventory synchronization across channels Considerations Primarily focused on major U.S. marketplaces Best suited for brands actively investing in marketplace growth 2. BigCommerce Best for: Brands that want a powerful ecommerce storefront with built-in multichannel capabilities. BigCommerce is one of the most popular ecommerce platforms on the market and is often chosen by brands that prioritize their website experience. In addition to storefront management, it offers integrations with marketplaces, social commerce channels and other sales destinations. The platform is particularly strong in customization, B2B ecommerce and composable commerce strategies. Many merchants use BigCommerce as the center of their commerce ecosystem while connecting specialized tools for marketplace operations. Strengths Strong ecommerce storefront capabilities Flexible customization options Supports both B2C and B2B ecommerce Built-in multichannel selling tools Large partner ecosystem Considerations More storefront-focused than marketplace-focused Larger marketplace sellers may require additional operational tools 3. Sellercloud Best for: Businesses with large catalogs and complex operational requirements. Sellercloud combines inventory management, order management, purchasing and warehouse operations into a single platform. It's a popular choice among high-volume sellers looking for greater control over day-to-day ecommerce operations. The platform offers extensive customization options and supports a wide range of workflows, making it a strong fit for businesses with more sophisticated operational needs. ChannelEngine Best for: Brands focused on marketplace expansion, particularly internationally. ChannelEngine specializes in marketplace connectivity and helps brands distribute products across a large network of marketplaces worldwide. The platform is often used by businesses looking to expand into new marketplaces without managing each channel individually. It’s particularly well suited for brands pursuing international marketplace growth. Its extensive marketplace network and expansion-focused tools make it easier to launch products across new regions while managing marketplace operations from a centralized location. Strengths Extensive marketplace network Strong international marketplace support Marketplace onboarding and syndication tools Centralized marketplace management Well suited for expansion strategies Considerations More marketplace-focused than operations-focused Some businesses may require additional tools for inventory or fulfillment management 5. Rithum Best for: Enterprise brands managing a large and diverse channel strategy. Formerly known as ChannelAdvisor, Rithum is designed for brands that need to manage a large and diverse channel strategy, including marketplaces, retailers and other commerce partners. It is one of the largest and most established players in the commerce operations space. The platform is commonly used by enterprise organizations that need broad channel coverage, extensive integrations and support for large-scale commerce initiatives. Base.com Best for: Sellers looking for broad marketplace connectivity and operational flexibility. Base.com (formerly BaseLinker) combines marketplace integrations, order management, inventory synchronization and shipping tools in a centralized platform. It has gained significant traction among sellers looking for a centralized way to manage multiple channels and fulfillment processes. The platform is particularly well known for its large integration network, which includes marketplaces, ecommerce platforms, carriers and operational tools. Some prioritize marketplace growth, while others focus on storefront commerce, operational control, international expansion or enterprise-scale commerce management. Before selecting a platform, evaluate your channel strategy, operational complexity, and long-term growth goals. The right solution should not only support your current business, but also provide the flexibility and automation needed to scale efficiently as your ecommerce operation grows. Instead of jumping between marketplaces, ecommerce platforms, and operational systems, sellers can centralize day-to-day tasks and reduce manual work. What's the difference between multichannel and omnichannel ecommerce? The terms are often used interchangeably, but they're not quite the same. Multichannel ecommerce simply means selling across multiple channels, such as Amazon, Walmart, and your ecommerce website. Omnichannel ecommerce takes it a step further by creating a more connected customer experience across those channels. What features matter most when evaluating multichannel ecommerce software? The right choice depends on your channel strategy, growth plans and operational requirements. When is it time to invest in multichannel ecommerce software? A good rule of thumb is this: if you're spending more time managing channels than growing them, it's probably time to look at software. Many businesses invest in a multichannel platform when they expand to additional marketplaces, struggle with inventory synchronization or find themselves relying on manual processes that no longer scale.

title: Cencora's Bet: Sell the Warehouses, Buy the Physicians
summary: Cencora ranks #2 in MDM's 2025 Pharma & Healthcare list. The real story is what the distribution giant is shedding, and what it is buying instead.
body_text: Part of Distributor Playbooks — strategy teardowns of every company on the 2025 MDM Top Distributors lists . Cencora lands at #2 in Modern Distribution Management's 2025 Top Distributors ranking for Pharma & Healthcare, on roughly $255.7 billion in 2024 revenue per MDM's report. That number alone tells you it moves about a fifth of every drug dispensed in the United States. What it does not tell you is that the company spent the past eighteen months quietly reversing the logic that built it: instead of adding more distribution categories, it is selling one off and buying its way into owning physician practices. The moat everyone already knows about The base business is scale, and scale in drug distribution is almost boring to describe. Cencora, McKesson, and Cardinal Health move the overwhelming majority of pharmaceuticals sold in the U.S., and the economics reward density: more warehouses, more delivery routes, tighter margins absorbed by volume. Cencora's version includes World Courier, a specialty and cold-chain logistics arm it bought in 2012 that handles clinical trial materials and temperature-sensitive biologics across more than 50 countries — a genuinely hard-to-replicate network for a category (cell and gene therapy, biologics) that is growing faster than pills in a bottle ever will again. That much is the standard playbook for a national pharma wholesaler. It is not the interesting part. The unbundling In January 2025, Cencora completed its acquisition of Retina Consultants of America , paying roughly $4.4 billion for an 85 percent stake in the largest management services organization in retina care, a specialty built around expensive, complex-to-administer treatments for macular degeneration. The company said the deal would let it "build on its leadership in specialty, expand its MSO solutions and drive differentiated value for stakeholders." Read plainly, that means Cencora now owns a piece of roughly 1,750 retina physicians and the 565-plus locations they practice out of. It is not distributing to those practices anymore. It is one of the practices. Then, thirteen months later, it did the opposite move on a different limb of the business. In February 2026, Cencora announced it would merge MWI Animal Health with Covetrus , folding its veterinary distribution unit — valued at $3.5 billion — into a combined company it will not control. Cencora walks away with $1.25 billion in cash, $800 million in preferred equity, and a 34.3 percent non-controlling stake. CEO Bob Mauch framed it as freeing Cencora to focus on "key growth priorities," and Covetrus CEO Ben Wolin talked about pairing MWI's distribution muscle with his company's technology platform. Put those two transactions side by side and the pattern is plain: Cencora is not trying to be the biggest distributor across every category anymore. It is trading breadth in commodity distribution categories, like animal health, for depth in specialty human healthcare, where owning the physician relationship and the drug supply chain around a single high-value therapy category is worth more than owning a warehouse network in a lower-margin adjacent business. That is the strategic tension worth naming plainly: a company that grew for two decades by adding distribution categories is now actively subtracting one, on the theory that vertical depth in specialty care beats horizontal breadth in general distribution. It is a bet that could look prescient in five years or could look like Cencora ceded a category to a competitor at exactly the wrong moment, if animal health turns out to be more valuable standalone than as a JV stake. How the company got built to make that bet Cencora's capacity to move that fast on portfolio surgery traces back to its own consolidation. The company was formed in 2001 when Bergen Brunswig merged with AmeriSource, combining two century-old drug wholesalers into what became AmerisourceBergen. Steven Collis took over as CEO in 2011 and, over 13 years, more than tripled revenue past $250 billion while building out the specialty and animal health arms through a string of deals: World Courier in 2012, MWI Veterinary for $2.5 billion in 2015, PharMEDium's compounding business the same year, H.D. Smith in 2018, and Alliance Healthcare from Walgreens for roughly $6.5 billion in 2021. In August 2023 the company renamed itself Cencora, and on October 1, 2024, Collis handed the CEO role to Robert Mauch , the company's COO and a 30-year pharma veteran who had founded Xcenda, a health economics consultancy Cencora acquired in 2007, before moving into operating roles. Collis stayed on as Executive Chair. It was Mauch, roughly a year into the job, who greenlit the Retina Consultants deal and the MWI-Covetrus merger back to back — a new CEO reshaping the portfolio faster than his predecessor did in over a decade of steady roll-up. What it adds up to The through-line is that Cencora no longer treats "distributor" as a fixed identity. It treats it as a starting position from which to move upstream into specialty care ownership where the drug is complex and the relationship is durable, while treating general distribution categories as things you can hold, or trade, depending on where the growth is. That is a harder story to tell in an annual report than "we deliver more pills to more pharmacies than anyone," but it is the one that actually explains the last two years of deal activity. Every distributor on MDM's list runs on the same unglamorous machinery underneath the strategy: catalogs that have to be accurate, branches that have to be stocked, and data that has to move as fast as the product does. This series keeps looking at how the largest players wire that machinery together.

title: Florida State Tax Guide
summary: This guide is for tax professionals who need to manage that reality. It focuses on the Florida taxes that create the most exposure in practice, including corporate income and franchise tax, sales and use tax, reemployment tax, and nexus rules.
body_text: Florida is often described as a “simple” tax state. No personal income tax at the state level. Familiar federal starting points. Relatively low headline rates. For tax professionals, that reputation is misleading and costly. Florida is not complex in the way California or New York can be. It is operationally strict. The Florida Department of Revenue enforces compliance through registrations, filing mechanics, electronic payment timing, and documentation standards that leave little margin for error. Many Florida assessments do not arise from aggressive tax positions. Many arise from procedural failures. A payment initiated too late in the ePay system. A missing resale certificate. A misclassified worker. An extension filed correctly but paid incorrectly. This guide is for tax professionals who need to manage that reality. It focuses on the Florida taxes that create the most exposure in practice, including corporate income and franchise tax, sales and use tax, reemployment tax, and the nexus rules that pull out-of-state businesses into Florida compliance. Because Florida risk is driven by administrative execution rather than technical complexity, practitioners need research that is Florida-specific, workflow-aware, and citation-driven. TaxGPT is designed for this environment, surfacing current Florida Department of Revenue guidance, portal rules, and procedural requirements with direct citations, so practitioners can validate compliance decisions inside their day-to-day workflow rather than relying on generalized tax research. Note: This guide reflects current-year Florida Department of Revenue guidance, portal requirements, and administrative procedures. Florida Tax Overview: What Every Practitioner Must Know Core Florida Tax Regimes Relevant to Practitioners Florida’s business tax system is concentrated in three areas that routinely intersect with federal compliance work. Corporate income or franchise tax applies to corporations, certain LLCs treated as corporations for federal purposes, financial institutions, and tax-exempt organizations with unrelated business taxable income. Florida generally uses federal taxable income as the starting point but applies its own exemption, apportionment, additions, and subtractions. Filing obligations are formal and unforgiving. Extension relief generally depends on whether a tentative tax is paid correctly and on time, and electronic payment rules are strictly enforced. Sales and use tax represents Florida’s most active enforcement area. The state imposes a 6% sales tax, with many counties layering a discretionary surtax. Collection responsibility depends on delivery location, service performance, or customer location, and errors are common where businesses operate across county lines or sell remotely. Use tax exposure from untaxed out-of-state purchases is a frequent audit finding, even for businesses that otherwise file income tax returns correctly. Reemployment tax , Florida’s unemployment tax regime, functions as the state’s primary payroll enforcement mechanism. Employer liability is triggered quickly, filing is quarterly, and worker classification issues are a consistent audit focus. From a risk perspective, reemployment tax in Florida plays a role similar to withholding tax in personal-income-tax states. Corporate Income and Entity Classification Reality Florida’s corporate income tax framework pulls in more entities than many practitioners initially expect. Corporations doing business, earning income, or deriving income from Florida sources must file Form F-1120. LLCs require careful classification analysis. An LLC treated as a corporation for federal purposes files as a corporation in Florida. A partnership-filed LLC may still trigger Florida filings indirectly when corporate owners are involved. A disregarded single-member LLC does not file separately, but its activity must be reflected on the owner’s Florida corporate return if the owner is a corporation. Florida allows a limited exemption on corporate income and requires estimated tax payments once liability thresholds are met. Multistate businesses must apportion income, and Florida sourcing rules for services, intangibles, and financial activity are often clarified through DOR Technical Assistance Advisements. Documentation supporting sourcing positions is not optional. It is expected. Sales and Use Tax Is Not a Side Issue Sales and use tax compliance often sits outside the core income tax workflow, but Florida audits do not treat it that way. Registration is required once taxable activity begins, not when revenue becomes material. Dealers must collect both state and applicable county surtax, apply surtax caps correctly, and remit on time. Electronic filing and payment thresholds are low, and payment timing rules require action by 5:00 p.m. ET on the applicable eServices deadline date. Waiting until the due date frequently results in late payments due to transaction-date and processing constraints.. A payment initiated on the due date itself is late. Remote sellers and marketplace activity have expanded Florida’s reach beyond its borders. Economic nexus rules bring out-of-state businesses into the Florida system even when no physical presence exists. Practitioners should assume that sales tax exposure will be examined whenever income tax or payroll issues surface. Reemployment Tax as an Enforcement Tool Florida’s reemployment tax applies once modest wage or employment thresholds are met. Registration, quarterly wage reporting, and payment are mandatory, and penalties accrue quickly for late or incomplete filings. Worker classification is a major risk area, particularly where businesses rely on contractors or seasonal labor. Florida coordinates reemployment tax with federal FUTA reporting, and failures at the state level can increase federal exposure through lost credits. Florida’s Lack of Personal Income Tax Does Not Reduce Audit Risk Florida does not impose a personal income tax, but that absence often creates a false sense of security. The DOR actively audits corporate income tax, sales and use tax, and reemployment tax. These audits follow structured timelines, apply statutory lookback periods, and result in assessments that include penalties and interest as a matter of course. The state’s enforcement posture is focused on compliance mechanics rather than aggressive tax theory, which makes procedural mistakes especially costly. Remote seller rules, local surtax complexity, and electronic payment enforcement have expanded audit scope in recent years. Businesses with clean federal returns still face meaningful Florida exposure when state-specific rules are not followed precisely. Practitioner Takeaway Florida risk is procedural, not computational. The state aggressively enforces registration requirements, filing deadlines, payment timing rules, and documentation standards. Practitioners who treat Florida as a “low-tax” state rather than a “high-compliance” state expose their clients to avoidable penalties. Florida vs High-Tax States: Where Practitioners Actually Get Burned In high-tax states, exposure often comes from complex rate structures and aggressive tax positions. In Florida, exposure comes from missed registrations, voided extensions, late electronic payments, incorrect surtax application, and undocumented sourcing. The tax itself may be modest, but the compliance penalties are not. For firms managing Florida exposure regularly, TaxGPT provides a centralized platform to research Florida corporate income tax, sales and use tax, and reemployment tax rules using current Department of Revenue guidance in one place. Florida Business Tax Filing Deadlines & Payment Requirements Corporate Income and Franchise Tax Filings Form F-1120 (corporations) Florida Form F-1120 is required for corporations subject to Florida corporate income or franchise tax, even if no tax is due for the year. A complete copy of the actual federal income tax return filed with the IRS must be attached to the Florida return. The due date for Form F-1120 is the later of: For tax years ending June 30, the first day of the fourth month following the close of the tax year. For all other taxable year ends, the first day of the fifth month following the close of the tax year. The fifteenth day following the original due date, without extension, of the related federal return. Florida does not waive filing obligations simply because liability is zero. Failure to file when required is treated as a compliance violation regardless of payment position. Extension Mechanics via Form F-7004 Florida does not recognize a federal extension by default. To extend the time to file Form F-1120, the taxpayer must file Florida Form F-7004 on or before the original Florida due date. An extension is valid only if all tentative tax due is paid timely. The extension is void if tentative tax is underpaid by more than the greater of $2,000 or 30 percent of the tax ultimately shown on the filed return. When an extension is voided, penalties and interest are assessed as if no extension had been granted. Extensions are generally granted for six months, or seven months for June 30 year-end filers. Only one extension may be granted per tax year. Estimated Tax Framework Thresholds Corporations that expect Florida corporate income or franchise tax liability to exceed $2,500 for the year must file a declaration of estimated tax and make installment payments using Florida Form F-1120ES. F-1120ES cadence Estimated tax is paid in four equal installments. For calendar-year filers, payments are due on May 31, June 30, September 30, and December 31. Florida generally expects estimated tax to be paid in four required installments. Uneven payments can trigger underpayment penalties. Critical Payment Mechanics Practitioners Cannot Miss Florida’s electronic payment system is a frequent source of penalties. The state does not treat electronic payments as timely based on submission date alone. Electronic payment deadlines Electronic payments require processing time. To be considered timely, the payment must be completed and a confirmation number received no later than 5:00 p.m. Eastern Time on the applicable deadline listed in the Florida eServices calendar. Deadlines falling on weekends or holidays are adjusted according to state rules, not federal banking conventions. Confirmation number requirement A payment is not considered made until the transaction is completed and a confirmation number is issued. Payments completed after 5:00 p.m. Eastern Time on the deadline are processed the next business day and are late, even if initiated earlier. 5:00 p.m. Eastern Time prior-day rule For corporate income and estimated tax payments, Florida generally requires electronic payments to be completed and confirmed by 5:00 p.m. Eastern Time on the applicable e-Services deadline date. As a best practice, practitioners should treat the effective cutoff as the business day before the statutory due date to reduce timing and processing risk. No automatic payment extension An extension of time to file is never an extension of time to pay. Tentative tax must be paid by the original Florida due date, regardless of federal extensions or filing relief. Florida enforces this separation strictly. Filing and Payment Summary Entity Type Form Due Date Extension Payment Rule C Corporations and taxable entities F-1120 1st day of 4th or 5th month after year-end, or 15 days after federal due date F-7004 filed by original due date with tentative tax paid Electronic payment completed with confirmation by 5:00 p.m. ET prior business day Corporations with expected liability over $2,500 F-1120ES May 31, June 30, September 30, December 31 (calendar year) Not applicable Equal installments, no annualization, strict electronic timing Penalties and Interest Reminder Florida penalties apply automatically. Late-filed returns are penalized at 10% per month, capped at 50 percent of tax due, or $50 per month up to $300 when no tax is due. Underpayment of tentative tax and estimated tax generally accrues penalties at an annualized rate of 12%. Interest accrues at a floating rate updated semiannually. Extension ≠ Payment Extension (Florida Enforces This Aggressively) Florida extensions protect only the filing deadline. If tentative tax is late or materially underpaid, the extension can be void. Payment timing and confirmation requirements are strictly enforced. In practice, most Florida penalties arise from payment timing failures, not incorrect tax calculations. Florida Tax Treatment by Entity Type Florida’s entity-level tax rules are closely tied to federal classification, but state filing and registration obligations often arise in ways practitioners do not expect. The absence of a personal income tax does not eliminate Florida compliance for pass-through entities or their owners. Instead, exposure is driven by nexus, entity classification, ownership structure, and activity within the state. Sole Proprietorships Federal filing backbone A sole proprietor reports business income and expenses on Schedule C attached to Form 1040, with self-employment tax calculated on Schedule SE. From a Florida income tax perspective, there is no separate personal income tax filing. That simplicity, however, ends at the registration and indirect tax level. Florida nexus considerations A sole proprietor may have Florida tax obligations even if the business is organized or headquartered elsewhere. Florida nexus can be created through employees or agents operating in the state, maintaining an office or place of business, assembling or servicing property, owning or leasing property in Florida, or delivering goods using company-owned or leased vehicles. Sales, use, and reemployment exposure Sole proprietors selling taxable goods or services, or renting taxable property in Florida, may be required to register for and collect sales and use tax. Use tax exposure is common when inventory or equipment is purchased out of state and used in Florida without tax paid at purchase. Reemployment tax applies once wage or employment thresholds are met. Paying at least $1,500 in wages in any calendar quarter or having at least one employee for any part of a day in 20 different weeks can trigger liability. Worker classification is a frequent audit issue, particularly where contractors are used. Partnerships and LLCs Taxed as Partnerships Federal pass-through baseline Partnerships are pass-through entities for federal income tax purposes and file an information return, with income reported at the owner level. A domestic LLC with two or more members is treated as a partnership by default unless it elects corporate status. Single-member LLCs are disregarded for income tax purposes but remain separate entities for employment and certain other taxes. When Florida filings are triggered indirectly Florida requires a Partnership Information Return, Form F-1065, when a partnership is doing business, earning income, or deriving income from Florida sources and at least one partner is subject to Florida corporate income tax. This rule frequently pulls partnerships into Florida compliance solely because of their ownership structure. An LLC classified as a partnership must file Form F-1065 if one or more owners is a corporation. In those cases, the corporate owner is also required to file Florida Form F-1120 to report its share of the LLC’s income, even if the LLC itself does not owe Florida corporate tax. Sales, use, and payroll touchpoints Partnerships and LLCs may be required to register for Florida sales and use tax when selling taxable items or leasing property. Payroll activity can trigger reemployment tax obligations based on employee counts and wage thresholds, and misclassification risk applies equally to pass-through entities. S Corporations Federal S corporation treatment S corporations are pass-through entities for federal income tax purposes and file Form 1120-S. Income and losses flow through to shareholders, although certain items, such as built-in gains or excess passive income, may be taxed at the entity level under federal rules. Florida corporate income tax filing triggers S corporations generally do not pay Florida corporate income tax. However, Florida requires an S corporation to file and pay tax when it is subject to federal income tax at the corporate level. This can occur when built-in gains tax is reported on the federal return. In those cases, the S corporation must file Florida Form F-1120 or, if eligible, Form F-1120A. When S corporations are pulled into Florida compliance Even when no Florida income tax return is required, S corporations conducting business in Florida may have sales and use tax or reemployment tax obligations. Out-of-state S corporations frequently trigger Florida compliance through employees, property, offices, servicing activities, or in-state deliveries using company vehicles. C Corporations Form F-1120 requirements Corporations doing business, earning income, or deriving income from Florida sources are required to file Florida Form F-1120 and attach a complete copy of the federal return. Required schedules, including apportionment schedules, must be included. Late filing or underpayment results in automatic penalties and interest. Corporate income and franchise tax Florida imposes corporate income or franchise tax on corporations, including certain tax-exempt organizations with unrelated business income. Estimated tax payments are required once liability thresholds are met. Multistate corporations must apportion income using Florida’s property, payroll, and sales factors and apply Florida-specific exemptions and net operating loss rules. Consolidated return elections Florida permits consolidated filing for affiliated groups when the parent corporation is subject to the Florida Corporate Income Tax Code. The Florida consolidated group must mirror the federal consolidated affiliated group. Each member must consent by filing Florida Form F-1122, and the election must be made by the due date, including extensions. Once elected, consolidated filing generally applies in subsequent years. Water’s-edge versus worldwide concepts Florida does not impose a separate worldwide unitary combined reporting regime. Consolidated filing is tied directly to the federal affiliated group, and the membership of the Florida consolidated return must match the federal group. Income is apportioned using Florida’s statutory factors as reported on Schedule III, rather than through a standalone combined reporting framework. Florida Corporate Income / Franchise Tax Return Mechanics Florida computes corporate income tax starting with federal taxable income and then applies Florida-specific additions, subtractions, and apportionment to arrive at Florida net income. Additions and subtractions Federal taxable income is adjusted to “adjusted federal income” under Chapter 220. Common additions include state income taxes deducted federally, tax-exempt interest net of disallowed expenses, and Florida decoupling adjustments tied to federal legislative changes. Florida requires a full addback of federal bonus depreciation under IRC section 168(k) for assets placed in service before January 1, 2027. That addback is recovered through a seven-year subtraction schedule, beginning in the year of the addback. Qualified improvement property follows a separate adjustment framework and does not use the standard seven-year recovery. Florida also decouples from federal provisions allowing expanded deductions for restaurant business meals and expensing under IRC section 181 for film, television, and live theatrical productions. These differences must be tracked annually and supported with schedules. Subtractions include allowable net operating loss deductions, capital loss carryovers, excess charitable contributions, certain foreign-source dividends and inclusions, and other items specifically permitted by statute. Florida does not permit net operating loss or capital loss carrybacks under any circumstances. Form F-1120 reports additions and subtractions on Schedule I and Schedule II, with dedicated lines for major decoupling adjustments. Errors in these schedules are among the most common sources of DOR assessments. Apportionment Adjusted federal income is apportioned to Florida using a weighted three-factor formula: property at 25 percent, payroll at 25 percent, and sales at 50 percent. Apportionment is computed on Schedule III of Form F-1120. Certain industries are subject to modified apportionment rules, but most corporations must apply the standard formula consistently year to year. After apportionment, nonbusiness income allocated to Florida is added, and the Florida exemption is applied to arrive at Florida net income subject to tax. Florida applies apportionment before net operating loss deductions, which directly affects the amount of NOL available for carryforward. Consolidated Filing Eligibility and mechanics Florida permits consolidated filing for affiliated groups when the parent corporation is subject to the Florida Corporate Income Tax Code and the group files a federal consolidated return. The Florida consolidated group must be identical to the federal consolidated affiliated group. Florida does not allow a separate state-only consolidation. The consolidated election must be made by the return due date, including extensions. Once made, consolidated filing is mandatory for subsequent years and applies to new members as they enter the federal group. Consent forms and schedules Each subsidiary included in a Florida consolidated return must file Form F-1122 consenting to inclusion. This applies in the initial year and whenever a new member joins the group. An affiliations schedule identifying the group must also be attached, typically federal Form 851 or its Florida equivalent. Missing or incomplete consents are a frequent basis for DOR adjustments. Net Operating Losses Carryforward only, no carryback Florida conforms to federal timing rules for net operating losses but expressly prohibits carrybacks. Losses must be carried forward and used in future years. Losses generated in taxable years beginning before January 1, 2018 may be carried forward for up to 20 years. Losses generated in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2017 carry forward indefinitely. For taxable years beginning after December 31, 2020, Florida applies a stacking approach. Pre-2018 carryovers are applied first and may offset 100 percent of Florida tentative apportioned adjusted federal income. Post-2017 carryovers are then applied, subject to an 80 percent limitation. Apportionment interaction Florida applies net operating loss deductions after apportionment. The Florida NOL carryover is generally limited to the federal NOL multiplied by the Florida apportionment fraction, adjusted for Florida-specific decoupling items. Other carryover deductions must be applied before the Florida NOL deduction. Failure to apply apportionment correctly to NOLs is a common audit issue. Penalties and Interest Posture Florida penalties are automatic and statutory. Late-filed returns are penalized at 10 percent per month or fraction thereof, capped at 50 percent of the tax due. If no tax is due, the penalty is $50 per month, up to $300. Corporations expecting more than $2,500 in annual tax must make estimated payments using Form F-1120ES. Underpayment of estimated tax is assessed at an annual rate of 12 percent. Underpayment of tentative tax during an extension period is also subject to a 12 percent annual penalty and may void the extension entirely. Interest accrues at a floating rate updated semiannually and applies independently of penalties. Amended Returns Amended Florida corporate returns are filed on Form F-1120X. This form is commonly used to reflect IRS audit adjustments or federal amended returns. Supporting federal documentation, such as a signed IRS Revenue Agent Report, must be attached along with updated Florida schedules. Florida generally requires refund claims to be filed within three years. When a federal change occurs, Florida imposes specific reporting timelines, including a 60-day reporting window and a two-year limitation period for certain adjustments. Amended returns must respect Florida’s prohibition on loss carrybacks. Practitioner Focus What commonly triggers DOR adjustments The most frequent Florida adjustments arise from missed or incorrect decoupling entries, particularly bonus depreciation, qualified improvement property, business meals, and IRC section 181 addbacks. Apportionment errors, including inconsistent factor computation and misclassification of business versus nonbusiness income, are also heavily scrutinized. Consolidated filing defects are another recurring issue, especially when the Florida group does not exactly match the federal group or when required consent forms are missing. Net operating loss errors, such as improper carrybacks or failure to apply the post-2020 stacking and limitation rules, routinely generate assessments. Estimated tax underpayments trigger penalties even when the annual return is ultimately correct. Documentation expectations Florida expects complete and organized filings. A copy of the actual federal return filed with the IRS must be attached, along with all relevant federal schedules. Consolidated returns must include all Forms F-1122 and the appropriate affiliations schedule. Taxpayers should maintain detailed schedules tracking net operating loss origination, apportionment fractions, usage, and remaining carryovers. Similar schedules should be retained for all decoupling adjustments, including bonus depreciation addbacks and multi-year subtractions. For amended returns, supporting federal audit or amendment documentation is required. In Florida, incomplete documentation is treated as a substantive compliance failure. Proper schedules and attachments are often the difference between a routine processing review and a formal assessment. Florida Sales & Use Tax: What Income Tax Practitioners Must Spot When Registration Is Required Florida requires registration before a business may collect, report, and remit sales and use tax. Registration is triggered by engaging in taxable activity, not by revenue size or profitability. Common registration triggers include: Selling taxable tangible personal property at retail or wholesale, including sales made through internet, catalog, or other remote channels. Preparing or selling food or drinks for immediate consumption, whether from a permanent location or a temporary or event-based setup. Renting or leasing taxable tangible personal property, or charging taxable admissions or memberships. Renting or leasing transient accommodations, parking spaces, boat or aircraft storage, and similar taxable rentals. Acting as a contractor that improves real property or fabricates components incorporated into real property, which may require self-accrual of tax on materials. Nonprofit organizations are not exempt from registration merely because they hold exemption certificates for purchases. If a nonprofit sells taxable items or services, or leases or rents commercial real property or transient accommodations, Florida requires registration and ongoing sales tax compliance. Once registered, the Department issues a Certificate of Registration and an Annual Resale Certificate for Sales Tax, both of which play a central role in ongoing compliance and audits. Use Tax Exposure From Out-of-State Purchases Use tax is one of the most overlooked Florida exposure areas. When a business purchases taxable items from out-of-state vendors that do not charge Florida tax and then brings those items into Florida for use, storage, or consumption, Florida use tax is generally due. Practitioner review should focus on accounts payable activity and fixed asset purchases from vendors that do not collect Florida tax. Common examples include equipment, supplies, and materials purchased online or from out-of-state suppliers. Failure to self-accrue use tax routinely results in audit assessments. In some cases, businesses may apply for a direct pay permit, allowing them to self-accrue and remit use tax directly to the Department rather than paying tax to vendors. This can streamline compliance for contractors and businesses with frequent taxable purchases used in Florida projects. Marketplace Facilitator Rules Florida’s marketplace laws assign collection responsibility based on how sales are structured, not simply on branding or platform use. A marketplace is any physical or electronic medium through which tangible personal property is offered for sale. A marketplace provider is a party that both lists or advertises a seller’s products and collects payment from the customer, transmitting all or part of that payment to the seller. This distinction is critical. If a platform collects customer payments and remits them to sellers, it is generally responsible for collecting and remitting Florida sales tax on those transactions. If the platform does not collect payment, and customers pay sellers directly or through a separate finance arrangement, the platform may not be treated as a marketplace provider. In those cases, the seller remains responsible for Florida registration and tax collection. Practitioners should ask a simple but decisive question when clients sell through platforms: who collects the customer’s payment and transmits it to the seller? The answer usually determines who bears Florida sales tax responsibility. Resale Certificates and the Annual Renewal Cycle Florida issues an Annual Resale Certificate for Sales Tax to registered dealers each calendar year. These certificates must be renewed annually and provided to vendors to support tax-free purchases for resale. Practitioners should confirm that clients print and use the current year’s certificate and understand that prior-year certificates are not valid. Florida provides online tools for printing and verifying resale certificates, and vendors are expected to verify certificate validity. Nonprofits follow a different cycle. Consumer’s Certificates of Exemption generally expire after five years and are renewed through a review process. These certificates apply to exempt purchases, not resale activity, and should not be confused with resale certificates. Substantiation Requirements Practitioners Must Enforce Sales tax audits often turn on documentation rather than substantive tax law. Vendors must retain proof of valid resale certificates for untaxed sales made for resale. Florida provides verification systems, but the burden of substantiation remains with the taxpayer. For nonprofits, exempt purchases should be paid directly with organization funds to preserve the exemption.. Purchases made with personal funds, even if later reimbursed, are taxable and routinely disallowed on audit. Registered dealers must be able to produce current resale certificates, exemption documentation, and supporting sales records promptly when requested. Audit Failure Patterns Florida’s sales and use tax audits follow a structured process, and procedural missteps can severely limit a taxpayer’s ability to contest an assessment. Failure to provide requested records allows the Department to issue estimated assessments based on the best information available. These estimates are treated as correct unless the taxpayer can prove otherwise. Records withheld during the audit or protest phase may be excluded from evidence later, absent good cause. When the Department issues administrative subpoenas for records and the taxpayer fails to comply, Florida law creates a rebuttable presumption that the Department’s proposed assessment is correct and that withheld records would be adverse to the taxpayer’s position. Certain industries face heightened consequences. Dealers selling alcoholic beverages or tobacco who fail to produce required records risk suspension of their resale certificates, publication on Department lists, and potential suspension or revocation of related licenses. Practitioner Takeaway Income tax practitioners are often the first line of defense against Florida sales and use tax exposure. Confirm registration when taxable activity exists, identify use tax liabilities from out-of-state purchases, clarify marketplace roles, and enforce resale certificate discipline. In Florida, sales tax audits are documentation-driven, and failures in recordkeeping routinely result in assessments that are difficult to unwind. Florida Nexus & Out-of-State Business Triggers Florida’s nexus standards are activity driven and applied broadly. Businesses do not need to be organized in Florida, generate significant Florida revenue, or maintain a permanent office to create filing and registration obligations. From the Department of Revenue’s perspective, in-state activity is a key driver of nexus and compliance responsibility.. For out-of-state businesses, nexus analysis is often the starting point for Florida exposure. Activities That Create a Florida Business Connection A business based outside Florida establishes a Florida business connection when it engages in certain in-state activities. Common nexus-creating activities include: Employees or agents in Florida Having employees, agents, or independent contractors conducting sales or other business activities in Florida points to nexus. The Department does not distinguish between revenue-generating and support roles when evaluating in-state presence. Installation or servicing activities Assembling, installing, repairing, or servicing products in Florida establishes nexus, even when sales contracts are executed elsewhere. Short-term work can “trigger registration/collection obligations for the period of activity.” Property ownership or leasing Owning, renting, or leasing real property or tangible personal property in Florida creates nexus. This includes equipment, inventory, or other assets located in the state for business use. In-state deliveries using company vehicles Delivering goods into Florida using company-owned or leased trucks is a nexus-creating activity. Delivery method matters. Use of common carriers is treated differently from company-controlled transportation. These activities are evaluated independently. A single qualifying activity is sufficient to establish a nexus. Registration Implications Across Florida Taxes Once nexus is established, Florida generally expects registration and compliance across multiple tax regimes. Practitioners should evaluate each tax separately rather than assuming a single registration covers all obligations. Corporate income and franchise tax An out-of-state corporation doing business in Florida is generally required to file Florida Form F-1120. Florida specifically treats an out-of-state corporation that is a partner in a Florida partnership as subject to the Florida Corporate Income Tax Code, even if the corporation has no other Florida activity. Nexus created through employees, property, or servicing activities typically triggers corporate income tax filing obligations. Sales and use tax Out-of-state businesses with Florida nexus are required to register for sales and use tax when they sell taxable goods or services delivered into Florida. Employees or agents in Florida, installation or servicing activity, property ownership, and company-truck deliveries are all cited by the Department as common registration triggers. Remote sellers and marketplace facilitators are subject to Florida’s electronic filing and payment requirements and must comply with Florida’s administrative systems once nexus exists. Reemployment tax Reemployment tax liability is triggered by relatively low thresholds once employees are present. Paying at least $1,500 in wages in any calendar quarter or having one or more employees for any part of a day in 20 different weeks generally creates liability. Separate thresholds apply for agricultural, domestic, nonprofit, and governmental employers. Worker classification is critical. Employees are subject to the employer’s direction and control, including corporate officers and individuals performing services for LLCs treated as corporations. Misclassifying workers as independent contractors can result in retroactive tax, penalties, and interest. Employers that meet liability thresholds must register and file quarterly Employer’s Reports using Form RT-6, with electronic filing required for certain employers. Practitioner Takeaway Florida nexus is established through activity, not intent. Out-of-state businesses frequently trigger Florida compliance through routine operational decisions such as sending employees into the state, installing equipment, or delivering goods with company vehicles. Once nexus exists, registration and filing obligations often span corporate income tax, sales and use tax, and reemployment tax. Early identification and prompt registration are the most effective ways to control Florida exposure and avoid cascading penalties. For practitioners comparing Florida nexus standards against other states, TaxGPT matrix can help map where Florida’s procedural enforcement differs from income-tax states and where multi-state compliance risks overlap.

title: Cosmic Rundown: SpaceX Buys Cursor, Chrome Kills Ad Blockers, Fable 5 Drama
summary: SpaceX acquires Cursor for $60B. Chrome's next update kills ad blockers. The US government pulls Fable 5 offline over a simple prompt. Here's what developers need to know.
body_text: SpaceX Acquires Cursor for $60 Billion SpaceX has agreed to acquire Anysphere, the company behind Cursor, for $60 billion in stock . The deal comes days after SpaceX's IPO and represents the largest acquisition in AI developer tooling history. Cursor had most recently raised at a $9 billion valuation. The exit represents roughly a 6.7x return on that round. The Hacker News discussion is running with questions about data privacy, pricing changes, and whether Cursor's rapid iteration pace will survive inside a larger organization. If you depend on Cursor for daily coding, now is a good time to review what data leaves your machine and whether your workflow survives a potential pricing or policy shift. Local Models Are Good Now Vicki Boykis published "Running local models is good now" , arguing that local LLMs have crossed a usability threshold for daily development work. The timing is notable. Yesterday's front page featured an Ask HN thread with over 500 comments asking whether anyone has successfully replaced Claude or GPT with a local model for daily coding. The consensus: for many tasks, yes. The structural argument is simple. If your AI coding assistant gets acquired, repriced, or policy-changed, a local model is the fallback that nobody can take away. The discussion on Hacker News digs into specific models, hardware requirements, and the tradeoffs. Chrome Update Kills Ad Blockers Google Chrome's next update will close the door on popular ad blockers . The change finalizes Chrome's transition to Manifest V3, which restricts the extension APIs that ad blockers like uBlock Origin rely on. The Hacker News thread is predictably heated. The practical advice: if you depend on ad blocking, Firefox still supports Manifest V2 extensions. For publishers and content teams, the shift is a double-edged sword. More users may see ads, but user trust in the browsing experience is taking another hit. Fable 5 Pulled Over "Fix This Code" Prompt The US government suspended access to Fable 5 and Mythos 5 after researchers demonstrated that a simple "fix this code" prompt could bypass safety guardrails. The models were not jailbroken in the traditional sense. They just followed instructions. The discussion raises questions about what "safe" means when models are trained to be helpful. If your production workflows depended on Fable 5 or Mythos 5, they are offline effective immediately. Quick Hits Banned book library in a light bulb. A developer built a banned book library inside a Wi-Fi smart light bulb . The discussion covers the technical implementation and the broader implications for censorship resistance. LinkedIn job offer backdoor. A security researcher documented a backdoor hidden in a LinkedIn job offer . The thread is a reminder that job seekers remain high-value targets for social engineering. John Carmack on Fabrice Bellard. Carmack tweeted that Fabrice Bellard is "almost certainly a better overall programmer" than himself. The Hacker News discussion turned into a celebration of Bellard's extraordinary body of work, from QEMU to FFmpeg to TinyCC. Microsoft x86 emulator fixed bad code during emulation. Raymond Chen shared a story about the x86 emulator team finding code so bad they fixed it during emulation . The discussion is full of similar war stories. What This Means for Content Teams The SpaceX/Cursor acquisition is the latest signal that consolidation in developer tooling is accelerating. Salesforce bought Contentful. OpenAI bought Windsurf. SpaceX bought Cursor. The tools developers use daily are increasingly owned by companies with different incentives than the founding teams. For content infrastructure, the same logic applies. If your CMS is one acquisition away from a pricing or policy change, your content is at risk. An API-first headless CMS with structured content, portable data, and no vendor lock-in is the architecture that survives these cycles. Sources: Hacker News , Reuters , 9to5Google , The Register

title: The Night the Lights Went Out: Engineering—And Experiencing—New York’s New Resilient Coastline
summary: Hurricane Sandy flooded Manhattan, but AI is helping build its defense. Explore how Bentley Systems and Arcadis are designing NYC's resilient new coastline.
body_text: On the night of October 29, 2012, Hurricane Sandy roared ashore in New Jersey, driving a wall of water toward one of the most densely populated coastlines in the world. New York City had braced for a flood, but what caught officials by surprise was the magnitude: The swell arrived at the peak of high tide, and the two forces together sent the East River surging over its banks with a fury no one anticipated. As water rushed upstream, the East River crested its banks and saltwater poured into the control room of Con Edison’s East River Generation Station, located at the northern edge of Manhattan’s East Village. Several blocks inland, at Con Edison’s Avenue A substation, senior operator Donnie Wilson watched the lights on his board flicker and die as the flooded power plant disconnected from the grid. “It was a scary situation just to sit in the dark,” he recalls. “I never experienced anything like that.” Con Edison is New York City’s largest utility. Its electrical system connects more than 3.5 million customers to energy sources and serves almost 40% of New York State’s electric demand, while covering only about 1% of the state’s geographic footprint. When the storm hit, firefighters and Con Edison’s emergency rescue group jumped into action. They floated rafts down Avenue C to pull power plant operators out of the rising water. “It was intense because nobody knew how bad the flood was going to be,” Wilson said. “We had to get rafts to get our personnel out during that time.” The power plant, the substation, and other facilities were severed from the grid, and roughly 200,000 customers lost power, some for several days. The Fortress on 14th Street Pedestrians enjoying the riverwalk, alongside the floodwalls, with Con Edison’s East River Generating Station in the background. Image Credits: BIG The East River Generation Station sits on the edge of a historically working-class, immigrant neighborhood of tenement blocks and housing projects. The homes are separated from the river by little more than a narrow strip of park and the scenic FDR Drive parkway. But the risk the river poses is changing. During the years since Sandy, engineers and construction crews have turned the power plant into what Jamie Brennan, Con Edison’s vice president of engineering, calls “a fortress” surrounded by floodwalls and massive floodgates. The neighborhood is also getting protection: The local park is being rebuilt as a flood barrier. Today, Con Edison is preserving the control room flooded by Sandy’s waters, as a kind of museum to the night the river came in. Wilson, the substation operator that night, walks visitors through the room. “It rose about this high,” he says, holding his hand at his waist. “All our electrical components down here were flooded.” In 2017, Con Edison moved the control room upstairs to a new, elevated facility. Outside, concrete walls and watertight doors now wrap the campus. Critical control wiring rides on tracks that operators hand-crank into the air 48 hours before the next big storm. New transformers sit on concrete pedestals 14 to 17 feet up. Just beyond Con Edison’s perimeter, the city’s wall is rising, too. The engineering firm Arcadis designed a 2.4-mile stretch of the East Side Coastal Resiliency project running from East 25th Street south to Montgomery Street, just below the Williamsburg Bridge. When completed, the barrier will be a continuous line of concrete walls, raised parks, and 18 massive floodgates. To design the gates, Arcadis used Bentley Systems’ STAAD structural engineering and analysis software, building virtual replicas that the team could test in extreme situations. Speed mattered, too. Roni Deitz, Arcadis’s global director of climate adaptation, says the software cut her team’s design time from 30 hours per gate to 30 minutes, while letting them simulate everything from storm-surge waves to a multi-ton garbage truck riding the flood and slamming into a gate. “Anything that could come at it, we need to be prepared for,” she says. East Side Coastal Resiliency project floodgate Bringing People Inside the Story Most New Yorkers will never see those gates closed, as they should be sheltering in a safe place when the next Sandy hits. To bring the system to a wider audience, Bentley sent photographer Aaron Huey to document the new infrastructure. Not with an ordinary camera, but with a 3D rig that produces Gaussian splats , a new and revolutionary way of capturing real-world spaces in three dimensions. Named for Carl Friedrich Gauss, the mathematician whose name graces the bell curve, the splats are mathematical functions that render each point in a scene as a soft, semi-transparent blob rather than a hard dot. Each splat carries data about its position, color, size, transparency, and orientation. Layered together, millions of them can reconstruct a 3D scene with striking realism, capturing thin wires, reflections, and even glass that changes appearance as the viewer moves around it—details that traditional polygon-based graphics often miss. To reconstruct the area around the plant, Bentley’s emerging technologies team, known as Bentley Labs and led by Greg Demchak, combined Huey’s splats with artificial intelligence (AI) and Unreal Engine, the gaming software now widely used in cinema and visual effects. Working from Huey’s captures of the old flooded control room, the new flood walls and the gates around the nearby Asser Levy Playground, the team built an immersive experience that lets a viewer watch the water rise to the level it reached the night of Sandy, then close the gates and see the new defenses hold. “Seeing is believing,” says Markus Sauerbeck, a senior developer in Bentley Labs who worked on the visualization. “We are using the latest emerging technology to let people understand much easier why these massive infrastructure projects are necessary for New York’s citizens.” Bentley recently presented the visualizations, which can be viewed in Apple Vision Pro, at London’s ATN conference and the Illuminate 2026 conference in Berlin. Plans are also in the works to bring the visualizations to New York. A 3D map shows Lower Manhattan with highlighted areas indicating the 100-year floodplain boundaries near the river and bridge. Image Credits: BIG “These models,” Huey says, “let us simulate what it looks like when the next Sandy arrives”—and what it will look like when, this time, the wall holds. An illustration showing the boundaries created by the flood walls. Image Credits: BIG FAQ: What happened to Con Edison's power plant during Hurricane Sandy? When the catastrophic hurricane and Nor’easter hit in 2012, a massive swell of saltwater poured directly into the control room of Con Edison’s East River Generation Station. The flooded power plant disconnected from the grid, forcing emergency rescues by raft and leaving roughly 200,000 customers sitting in the dark. How has the 14th Street Con Edison plant been rebuilt to survive the next storm? Engineers have transformed the facility into a resilient “fortress” wrapped in concrete floodwalls and watertight doors. The original flooded control room is now just a museum; critical operations were moved upstairs, transformers were elevated 14 to 17 feet, and operators can even hand-crank vital wiring out of harm’s way before a storm hits. What are Gaussian splats, and how do they help visualize New York City's coastline? Named after mathematician Carl Friedrich Gauss, Gaussian splats are a revolutionary 3D mapping method that renders data points as semi-transparent blobs rather than hard dots. Bentley Labs layered millions of these splats to capture hyper-realistic details of the new flood walls—like reflections and thin wires—that traditional polygon graphics usually miss.

title: NASA Selects Rocket Lab to Launch Sun, Earth Sciences Missions
summary: The PolSIR and TSIS-2 missions will fly across three dedicated Electron launches from Q1 2027 to meet each mission’s time-sensitive requirements LONG BEACH, Calif., June 25, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Rocket Lab Corporation (Nasdaq: RKLB), a global leader in launch services and space systems, today
body_text: NASA Selects Rocket Lab to Launch Sun, Earth Sciences Missions June 25, 2026 PDF Version The PolSIR and TSIS-2 missions will fly across three dedicated Electron launches from Q1 2027 to meet each mission’s time-sensitive requirements LONG BEACH, Calif., June 25, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Rocket Lab Corporation (Nasdaq: RKLB), a global leader in launch services and space systems, today announced it has been selected by NASA to provide three Electron launches for two separate NASA missions - PolSIR and TSIS-2 – from early next year. Rocket Lab’s extensive flight heritage across more than 90 launches, Electron’s proven deployment accuracy, and the company’s ability to meet the tight turnaround schedules for both missions were key driving factors behind Rocket Lab being selected as the launch provider. Rocket Lab will fly two back-to-back Electron launches for NASA’s PolSIR mission from Launch Complex 1 in New Zealand no earlier than June 2027. A separate Electron launch for NASA’s TSIS-2 mission will take place from the same launch site in early 2027. PolSIR Electron will deploy two identical CubeSats for the PolSIR (Polarized Submillimeter Ice-cloud Radiometer) mission to study ice clouds at high altitudes in the tropics and sub-tropics: how they form, why they change throughout the day, and how much ice they contain. The data gathered by PolSIR will be used to inform Earth system models to make better predictions about Earth’s weather across the globe. The PolSIR mission requires both satellites to fly in separate, 52-degree inclination, non-sun synchronous orbits that will allow NASA scientists to make comparisons across daily, seasonal, and annual cycles of ice clouds. Electron’s excellent track record for precise orbital deployment and ability to deliver satellites within meters of their target – versus the industry standard of kilometer-level deployment accuracy - is being leveraged to meet NASA’s unique requirements of this mission. TSIS-2 NASA’s TSIS-2 (Total and Spectral Solar Irradiance Sensor-2) mission will see a single satellite launched by Electron to conduct Sun-Earth energy science. TSIS-2’s measurements of the Sun’s brightness at the top of Earth’s atmosphere, as well as the distribution of that energy over ultraviolet, visible, and infrared wavelengths, can be used by scientists to predict Earth’s ozone layer recovery or provide air quality forecasts: real-life examples of the benefits space science missions like TSIS-2 can have for day-to-day life. This mission exemplifies Electron’s unique capability and value in providing a reliable and responsive launch service dedicated for small satellites. NASA has booked the mission to launch on Electron in just seven months from contract signing to meet the time-sensitive requirements of the mission. Rocket Lab founder and CEO, Sir Peter Beck, says: “Electron has become synonymous with reliability, precise orbital accuracy, and on-demand launch capability and we’ve been delivering this for NASA missions for almost a decade. We’re proud to deliver this once again for PolSIR and TSIS-2.” Alongside PolSIR and TSIS-2, other upcoming NASA missions to be launched by Rocket Lab include the agency’s Aspera mission: an astrophysics mission to study the formation and evolution of galaxies and provide new insights into how the universe works. Later this year, Rocket Lab is also scheduled to deploy its own Photon spacecraft on Electron for NASA’s LOXSAT mission: a demonstration of in-space refueling technologies that could come into play for future Moon missions and human exploration to Mars. body_text: CervoMed Secures New U.S. Patent Protecting Use of Neflamapimod in Pure Dementia with Lewy Body Patients into 2042 June 18, 2026 PDF Version BOSTON, June 18, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- CervoMed Inc. (NASDAQ: CRVO), a clinical-stage biotechnology company developing treatments for age-related brain disorders (CervoMed or the Company), today announced that it has received a notice of allowance from the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) related to a new patent protecting the Company’s use of its drug candidate, neflamapimod, for the treatment of dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) in patients with no substantial Alzheimer’s disease-like tau pathology, also known as “pure DLB”. The patent will cover the treatment of DLB without substantial tau pathology, which can be characterized by plasma levels of pTau or brain imaging, and is expected to provide intellectual property protection into 2042 and potentially longer with patent term extension. The patent is designed to protect the Company’s strategy targeting the treatment of patients with pure DLB. Currently, there are no approved treatments for DLB in the United States or European Union. About CervoMed CervoMed is a clinical-stage company developing treatments for age-related brain disorders. Its lead drug candidate, neflamapimod, is an oral small molecule targeting critical disease processes underlying degenerative disorders of the brain by inhibiting a key enzyme involved in neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration. CervoMed’s recently completed Phase 2b RewinD-LB trial evaluated neflamapimod in patients with DLB, enriched for those without Alzheimer’s disease (AD) co-pathology, and the Company announced alignment with the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) on a potential registration path for neflamapimod in DLB in November 2025. Initiation of a Phase 3 trial in DLB is subject to the establishment of a partnership and/or additional financing. CervoMed also recently completed enrollment in its ongoing Phase 2a clinical trial evaluating neflamapimod in nonfluent variant primary progressive aphasia (nfvPPA), a subtype of frontotemporal disorders, from which interim biomarker data is anticipated in the early fourth quarter of 2026, and expects the first patient to be dosed with neflamapimod in the EXPERTS-ALS Phase 2a clinical trial in the fourth quarter of 2026. body_text: Eversource Energy Completes the Sale of Aquarion Water Company June 30, 2026 PDF Version HARTFORD, Conn. and BOSTON, June 30, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Eversource Energy (NYSE:ES) (“Eversource”) today announced that it has successfully completed the sale of Aquarion Water Company (“AWC”), consistent with all regulatory terms and requirements, to Aquarion Water Authority (“AWA”), a quasi-public corporation and political subdivision of the State of Connecticut and a standalone water authority alongside the South Central Connecticut Regional Water Authority (“RWA”).
